analogy.p: Think of the nucleus as a locked reference library holding one enormous recipe book (the DNA). The books can never leave, so a cook who wants a single recipe (a gene) makes a photocopy of that one page (the mRNA) and carries it into the kitchen (the cytoplasm). In the kitchen the chef (the ribosome) reads the copy three words at a time, and assistants (carrier molecules) fetch exactly the ingredient (amino acid) named by each word, in the right order. The finished dish (the protein) is then shaped and plated so it can do its job. A typo in the recipe (a mutation) can change one ingredient, so the dish comes out differently, or sometimes the same. The analogy breaks down because a real recipe is read by a thinking cook, whereas a ribosome follows the code mechanically and the 'ingredients' are chemically matched by the shape of the carrier molecules.
analogy.t: A recipe book in a locked library

bullets: **DNA** is a double-helix polymer found in the nucleus, organised into chromosomes; a **gene** is a small section of a chromosome.
Each gene contains the code for making **one specific protein** (a specific sequence of amino acids).
The whole of the DNA of an organism is its **genome**; the human genome has around 20 000 protein-coding genes.
The flow of information is: **DNA (gene) -> mRNA copy -> ribosome -> protein chain -> folded protein -> function**.
DNA itself never leaves the nucleus; only a copy of one gene (mRNA) does.
Protein synthesis happens all the time in living cells, as proteins are constantly needed to grow, repair and run reactions.
Link: this is how a change in DNA (a mutation) can change a characteristic such as enzyme activity.
core.h: The big picture: from gene to characteristic
core.p: Every cell in your body contains the same genome, but a cell can only use that information by building proteins. A **gene** is a short section of DNA that holds the code for one particular protein, so protein synthesis is the process that turns the instructions in DNA into working molecules. The proteins a cell makes decide what it can do (enzymes), how it is built (structural proteins) and how it communicates (hormones, receptors). That is why genes control **phenotype**: gene -> protein -> characteristic. Protein synthesis is the key link between the genotype and the phenotype in this topic.

bullets: **Enzymes** are protein catalysts that speed up reactions (for example amylase, protease, catalase).
**Hormones** such as insulin are proteins that act as chemical messengers in the blood.
**Antibodies** are proteins whose shape is complementary to a specific antigen on a pathogen.
**Structural proteins** such as collagen (strong skin, tendons and bone) and keratin (hair and nails) give strength.
**Haemoglobin** is a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen; receptor and carrier proteins in membranes are also proteins.
There are **20 different amino acids**; different orders give different proteins with different shapes and functions.
Proteins are made of amino acids joined in a chain, just as DNA is made of nucleotides.
core.h: What proteins are and why they matter
core.p: Proteins are large molecules (polymers) made from long chains of smaller units called **amino acids**. There are 20 different amino acids found in living things, and the order in which they are joined is what makes one protein different from another. A protein with 200 amino acids can be arranged in an astronomical number of ways, which is why there can be so many different proteins in a body. Because the chain folds up, its final three-dimensional shape depends entirely on the amino acid sequence.

bullets: **A sequence of three bases (a triplet) is the code for a particular amino acid.**
The **order of the bases** controls the **order in which amino acids are assembled** to make a particular protein.
Four bases taken three at a time give 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 possible triplets, which is more than enough for 20 amino acids (so more than one triplet can code for the same amino acid).
Some triplets act as 'start' and 'stop' signals telling the cell where a protein begins and ends.
Number of bases in the coding part of a gene = **3 x number of amino acids** in the protein (ignoring any stop triplet).
Number of amino acids = number of bases / 3.
The base pairs in DNA are A with T and C with G (complementary base pairing); this is how an accurate copy of a gene can be made.
core.h: The genetic code: bases, triplets and amino acids
core.p: DNA contains four bases (A, C, G and T) arranged in a particular order along each strand. The order of these bases is the code. The code is read in groups of three bases called a **triplet**, and each triplet codes for one amino acid. This is why the order of bases in a gene controls the order in which amino acids are assembled, and so decides which protein is made. Different genes have different base sequences, so they code for different proteins.

bullets: DNA is too large to pass through the nuclear pores and must stay protected in the nucleus.
**mRNA is a copy of one gene**; it is made in the nucleus using the base sequence of the gene.
mRNA is much shorter than a chromosome and is single stranded (DNA is double stranded).
mRNA leaves the nucleus through a **nuclear pore** and moves to a ribosome in the cytoplasm.
Many copies of mRNA can be made from one gene, so lots of protein can be made without risking the DNA.
mRNA is only temporary: it is broken down after use, so the cell can control how much of each protein it makes.
Because the mRNA is a copy, a mutation in the DNA gene produces a changed mRNA and therefore a changed protein.
core.h: Why a copy is needed: the role of mRNA
core.p: DNA is a very long and precious molecule that stays safely inside the nucleus, but proteins are built at **ribosomes** in the cytoplasm. The cell solves this problem by making a temporary working copy of just one gene. This copy is called **messenger RNA (mRNA)**. It is a shorter, single-stranded molecule that carries the code out of the nucleus through a nuclear pore to a ribosome. The mRNA then acts as the **template** that controls the order of amino acids.

bullets: Happens in the **nucleus**.
The DNA strands separate in the region of the gene so that the bases are exposed.
Complementary bases line up against the exposed bases to build the mRNA copy.
The mRNA strand then separates from the DNA, and the DNA strands rejoin.
The order of bases on the mRNA is therefore a complementary copy of the order of bases in the gene.
The mRNA then leaves the nucleus; the original DNA stays in the nucleus.
Exam tip: if the question asks where the copy is made, answer 'in the nucleus'.
core.p: The first stage takes place in the nucleus. The section of DNA that makes up the gene is used as a pattern to build a matching mRNA molecule, base by base, using complementary base pairing. The result is an mRNA strand whose base sequence is a complementary copy of the gene. This stage is called **transcription** in many textbooks; the AQA wording simply says that a copy of the gene is made. In either case, the information (the order of bases) has been copied exactly so that it can be moved.

bullets: **Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes**, according to a template (the mRNA).
The ribosome moves along the mRNA reading **one triplet at a time**.
**Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids** to add to the growing protein chain in the correct order.
Each carrier molecule only fits one particular triplet, so the right amino acid goes in the right place.
The amino acids are joined together by bonds to form a chain (a protein chain or polypeptide).
The chain keeps growing until the end of the gene is reached and the protein chain is complete.
Ribosomes are found free in the cytoplasm and attached to rough endoplasmic reticulum; they are not membrane-bound organelles.
core.h: Step 2 - the ribosome and carrier molecules
core.p: In the cytoplasm the mRNA attaches to a **ribosome**. Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template, and the template is the mRNA. The ribosome reads the mRNA in sets of three bases. **Carrier molecules** each bring one specific amino acid to the ribosome and match up with the correct triplet on the mRNA. As each amino acid arrives it is joined to the growing chain, so the amino acids are added in exactly the order specified by the mRNA. This stage is often called **translation**.

bullets: The completed chain **folds** into a **unique 3D shape**.
The shape depends on the **sequence of amino acids**, so the sequence of bases in the gene ultimately determines the shape.
**Enzymes**: the shape of the active site is complementary to the substrate (lock and key), so only that substrate fits.
**Antibodies**: the binding site has a shape complementary to one specific antigen.
**Hormone receptors** have a shape that fits only the matching hormone.
**Structural proteins** such as collagen fold or twist into strong fibres.
If the shape is wrong, the protein cannot work, even if the correct amino acids are present.
core.h: Step 3 - folding to a unique shape
core.p: When the protein chain is complete it is released from the ribosome and **folds up to form a unique shape**. The folding is not random: attractions between particular amino acids in the chain pull it into a specific three-dimensional structure. This unique shape is what enables a protein to do its job. Change the order of amino acids and you may change the shape, and so change the function.

bullets: The gene (section of DNA in the nucleus) holds the code as a sequence of bases.
A copy of the gene is made as **mRNA** in the nucleus.
mRNA moves out of the nucleus (through a nuclear pore) to a **ribosome**.
The ribosome reads the mRNA as a **template**, three bases at a time.
**Carrier molecules** bring the specific amino acids in the correct order.
The amino acids are joined into a chain.
The chain **folds** into a **unique shape**.
The protein does its job (enzyme, hormone, antibody, structural component).
core.h: Summary of the whole process in order
core.p: Putting the stages together gives a sequence you can reproduce for a 4 or 6 mark question. Each statement should link to the next with a clear reason, because mark schemes reward the idea that the order of the bases decides the order of the amino acids, which decides the shape and the function. Always say where each stage happens.

bullets: Not all parts of DNA code for proteins.
Non-coding parts can **switch genes on and off**.
Variations (mutations) in these areas may **affect how genes are expressed**.
This explains why different cell types (nerve, muscle, skin) have the same genes but make different proteins.
A mutation in a switch region could stop a gene being made, or make too much of the protein, without altering the protein's structure.
Exam tip: the phrase to learn is 'switch genes on and off'.
Link: cell differentiation in stem cells depends on which genes are switched on.
core.h: Not all DNA codes for proteins: non-coding DNA
core.p: Only part of the genome is made of genes that code for proteins. Large regions of DNA do not code for proteins at all. These **non-coding** parts of DNA are not wasted: some of them can **switch genes on and off**, which means they control **gene expression**, in other words whether a gene is used to make its protein in a particular cell at a particular time. Variations in these regions can therefore affect how genes are expressed, even though no amino acid sequence is changed.

bullets: A mutation is a **random change in the DNA base sequence**.
**Mutations occur continuously.**
**Most mutations do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly**, so the phenotype is not affected.
**A few mutations influence the phenotype.**
**Very rarely a mutation leads to a new phenotype.**
If the new phenotype is suited to a change in the environment, it can lead to relatively **rapid change** in the species (natural selection).
Types of change: **substitution** (one base swapped for another), **insertion** (extra base added) and **deletion** (a base lost).
Most mutations are neutral; some are harmful, and a tiny number are beneficial.
core.h: Mutations: what they are and how often they happen
core.p: A **mutation** is a random change in the structure (base sequence) of DNA. Mutations occur continuously, because copying DNA for cell division is very accurate but not perfect. Most mutations do not alter the protein, or alter it very little, so they have no effect on the phenotype. A few influence the phenotype, and very rarely a mutation leads to a new phenotype. If that new phenotype is suited to a change in the environment it gives a survival advantage, which can lead to relatively rapid change in a species.

bullets: Mutation -> **changes the order of bases** in the gene.
-> may **alter the sequence of amino acids** in the protein.
-> the protein may **fold differently** and have a **different shape**.
-> the protein may **no longer function** (e.g. enzyme active site no longer complementary to the substrate).
A **substitution** changes at most one amino acid because the triplets either side are unchanged.
An **insertion or deletion** shifts every triplet after it (a frame shift), so many amino acids can change (Higher extension).
No effect if: the new triplet codes for the same amino acid, the mutation is in non-coding DNA, or the changed amino acid does not alter the shape.
Link: inherited disorders such as cystic fibrosis are caused by gene mutations that alter a protein.
core.h: How a mutation in a gene changes a protein
core.p: A mutation in a gene can change the order of the bases. That can change the triplet and so change the amino acid it codes for. If the amino acid sequence changes, the protein may fold differently and have a different shape. A different shape can mean that the protein can no longer do its job. For an enzyme, for example, a changed shape of the active site means the substrate no longer fits, so the reaction is not catalysed. A mutation does not always change the protein, since several triplets code for the same amino acid, or the mutation may be in a non-coding region.

bullets: Mutation is a source of **new alleles**, one cause of genetic variation (the others being sexual reproduction and recombination of alleles).
A new allele can code for a **different protein** giving a **different phenotype**.
A beneficial phenotype increases the chance of **survival and reproduction**.
Alleles for advantageous characteristics are more likely to be passed on, so become more common.
Example: bacteria can mutate to become resistant to an antibiotic; resistant bacteria survive treatment and reproduce.
Link: genetic engineering moves genes between organisms so that the same genetic code makes the same protein in a new host (the genetic code is nearly universal).
core.h: Linking protein synthesis to evolution and variation
core.p: Variation between individuals arises partly from mutations in DNA that create new alleles. New alleles give new proteins and new phenotypes. If a phenotype is better suited to its environment, individuals with it are more likely to survive and reproduce and pass the allele on, so it becomes more common over generations. This is the link between protein synthesis (a molecular process) and natural selection (a population process). Without mutation there would be no new alleles for natural selection to act on.

bullets: Bases in coding region = amino acids x 3.
Amino acids = bases / 3 (a sequence of 90 bases codes for 30 amino acids).
Split sequences into triplets from the start: e.g. ATGCCAGGT = ATG | CCA | GGT = 3 triplets = 3 amino acids.
Complementary strand: A pairs with T, C pairs with G (e.g. ATGCCA -> TACGGT).
To spot a mutation, compare the two sequences triplet by triplet and underline the changed base.
If only one triplet changes in a substitution, at most one amino acid is changed.
If a base is inserted or deleted, check how many triplets after that point are altered.
core.p: Questions on this topic often include simple data tasks. You may be asked to convert between the number of amino acids and the number of bases, to split a sequence into triplets, or to say what effect a changed base would have. Always show the working: divide or multiply by 3, and state what the answer means. When you are given a sequence before and after a mutation, compare it triplet by triplet to find exactly which triplet changed.

exam: Command words: **describe** = say what happens in order; **explain** = give the reasons (use 'so', 'because', 'therefore'); **suggest** = apply the ideas to a new situation.
1 mark: a single fact such as 'mRNA' (what carries the code out of the nucleus) or 'ribosome' (where proteins are made).
2 marks: usually a fact plus a link, for example 'a triplet of bases codes for one amino acid, so the order of bases controls the order of amino acids'.

3-4 mark 'explain how a mutation changes a protein': change in base sequence -> different amino acid(s) -> different shape (folds differently) -> no longer functions (active site no longer fits substrate).
6 mark protein synthesis questions: write in sequence, naming where each stage happens (nucleus, nuclear pore, ribosome) and finish with folding into a unique shape.
Use exact phrases: 'proteins are synthesised on ribosomes', 'carrier molecules bring specific amino acids', 'in the correct order', 'folds to form a unique shape', 'switch genes on and off'.
Always link the shape of the protein to its function; just saying 'it stops working' does not get the mark.
Calculation questions: multiply or divide by 3, show the working, and give the final answer with the right quantity (bases or amino acids).
Sequence questions: split into triplets with lines, then compare triplet by triplet; state which triplet changed and what that means.
Do not say 'DNA goes out of the nucleus' or 'the mutation makes the enzyme denature'; both lose marks.
Remember Higher tier only: this content is marked HT, so expect it on Higher papers (Paper 2 for this unit).

mistakes.r: DNA stays in the nucleus; a copy of the gene, mRNA, carries the code to the ribosome.
mistakes.w: DNA leaves the nucleus and goes to the ribosome.

mistakes.r: A sequence of three bases (a triplet) codes for one amino acid.
mistakes.w: Each base codes for one amino acid.

mistakes.r: Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
mistakes.w: Proteins are made in the nucleus.

mistakes.r: Most mutations have no effect; a few change the phenotype and very rarely give a new advantageous phenotype.
The mutation changes the base order, which changes the amino acid sequence, so the protein folds into a different shape and the active site no longer fits the substrate.
mistakes.w: The mutation changes the enzyme so it stops working.

mistakes.r: Denaturing is caused by high temperature or extreme pH; a mutation changes the amino acid sequence permanently.
Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to the ribosome in the order set by the mRNA.
mistakes.w: Carrier molecules make the amino acids.

mistakes.r: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein.
Non-coding DNA can switch genes on and off, affecting gene expression.

summary: Higher tier: you must be able to describe and explain how the base sequence of a gene is used to build a protein. A copy of the gene (mRNA) carries the code from the nucleus to a ribosome, where carrier molecules bring amino acids in the order the code specifies, and the finished chain folds into a unique shape. You also need to explain how mutations and non-coding DNA affect proteins and phenotype, because every characteristic of an organism ultimately depends on which proteins its cells make.

terms.d: A small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein.
The entire genetic material of an organism.
A polymer made of a chain of amino acids that folds into a unique shape; examples are enzymes, hormones, antibodies and structural proteins.
The monomer (building block) of proteins; there are 20 different ones, joined in a specific order.
The part of a DNA nucleotide that carries the code: A, C, G or T.
A sequence of three bases that codes for a particular amino acid.
A single-stranded copy of a gene that carries the code from the nucleus to a ribosome and acts as the template for protein synthesis.
The pattern (mRNA) on a ribosome that controls the order in which amino acids are joined.
The structure in the cytoplasm where proteins are synthesised.
A molecule that brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and adds it to the growing protein chain in the correct order.
A small opening in the nuclear membrane through which mRNA leaves the nucleus.
The rule that A pairs with T and C pairs with G in DNA, which allows an accurate copy of a gene to be made.
Parts of DNA that do not code for proteins; some can switch genes on and off.
Whether a gene is switched on and used to make its protein in a particular cell.
A random change in the structure (base sequence) of DNA.
The part of an enzyme whose shape is complementary to its substrate.
The characteristics of an organism, produced by the proteins made from its genes and by the environment.

worked.q: A gene codes for a protein containing 150 amino acids. (a) How many bases are in the coding region of the gene (ignore any stop triplet)? (b) A different coding sequence has 612 bases. How many amino acids does it code for? [3 marks]
steps: Three bases code for one amino acid.

worked.ans: The mutation changes one base in the second triplet, so a different amino acid may be coded for. This changes the order of amino acids, so the protein folds into a different shape. For an enzyme the active site is no longer complementary to the substrate, so the reaction is not catalysed and the protein no longer works.
worked.q: A section of a gene has the base sequence ATG CCA GGT TAC. A mutation changes it to ATG CTA GGT TAC. Explain how this could stop a protein from working. [4 marks]
steps: Identify the change: the second triplet changes from CCA to CTA (one base substituted).
Each triplet codes for one amino acid, so the second amino acid may be different.
A different amino acid sequence means the protein folds into a different shape.
If the shape changes, the active site (or binding site) may no longer fit its substrate (or be complementary), so the protein cannot do its job.

worked.ans: A copy of the gene is made in the nucleus as mRNA, using the order of bases in the gene. The mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore, while the DNA stays in the nucleus. The mRNA attaches to a ribosome in the cytoplasm and acts as a template. Each set of three bases (triplet) codes for one amino acid. Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to the ribosome, in the correct order, to add to the growing protein chain. The amino acids are joined together to make the protein chain. When the chain is complete it folds to form a unique shape, which allows the protein to do its job, for example as an enzyme, hormone or antibody.
worked.q: Describe how the information in a gene is used to make a protein. [6 marks]
steps: Start in the nucleus: a copy of the gene is made as mRNA.
Say mRNA leaves via a nuclear pore, DNA stays.
At the ribosome the mRNA is the template, read as triplets.
Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids in the correct order.
Amino acids joined into a chain; chain folds to a unique shape which lets the protein do its job.
